verdict.rationale: The lexical pattern across the cited corpus aligns the Spirit's presence with order and tested speech rather than unbounded ecstatic display. In 1 Cor 14:33 God is predicated negatively as not akatastasias (G0181, disorder, tumult, attested 5x in 1 Cor 14:33, 2 Cor 6:5, 2 Cor 12:20, Jas 3:16, Luke 21:9, always pejorative) and positively as eirenes (G1515, peace, 92 NT occurrences, pan-canonical), and 14:40 commands that all things be done euschemonos (G2156, decently, 3x in 1 Cor 14:40, Rom 13:13, 1 Thess 4:12, every NT use governing visible bodily conduct) and kata taxin (G5010 taxis, in arrangement). The immediate regulation in 14:27-32 makes the same pattern explicit lexically: G1329 diermeneutes (interpreter required), G1252 diakrino (others judge prophecy, 14:29), G5293 hypotasso (spirits of the prophets are SUBJECT to prophets, 14:32). Deut 18:20-22 supplies a verification test rather than a phenomenology of intensity, judging a self-asserted prophetic word by fulfillment and exposing presumptuous speech (zid H2102, zadon H2087). 1 John 4:1 commands dokimazete ta pneumata (G1381, test the spirits) precisely because many pseudoprophetai (G5578) have gone out, and 1 Thess 5:21 anchors the same dokimazo applied to prophetic utterance. Treating ecstatic phenomena as the normative criterion of the Spirit therefore runs against the dense, pan-canonical pattern of tested, orderly, fulfillment-checked speech.

scripture.force: God is predicated negatively against akatastasia (disorder, tumult, confusion, 5 NT occurrences all pejorative) and positively as the God of eirene (peace, 92 NT occurrences, pan-canonical Pauline and Johannine and Petrine usage). The genitive of quality construction ou estin akatastasias ho theos alla eirenes ties the divine character itself to peaceful order, making disorder in assembly inconsistent with the Spirit's source.

The closing imperative panta de euschemonos kai kata taxin ginestho directs that all things in corporate worship occur decently and according to arranged order. The adverb euschemonos (3 NT occurrences, every instance governing visible bodily conduct: Rom 13:13 walking properly, 1 Thess 4:12 walking properly toward outsiders, 1 Cor 14:40 corporate gifts) and the prepositional phrase kata taxin set a governing norm of seemliness and arrangement over the exercise of gifts described in the surrounding chapter. The third-person imperative ginestho expresses an enduring rule, not a one-time request.

The present imperative dokimazete ta pneumata ei ek tou theou estin (test the spirits whether they are from God) is grounded by hoti polloi pseudoprophetai exelelythasin eis ton kosmon. The same lemma dokimazo appears at 1 Thess 5:21 commanding dokimazete panta over prophetic utterance specifically, anchoring the test-the-spirits command as a pan-Pauline and Johannine norm. Spiritual claims are subjected to evaluation rather than received on manifestation, because false prophets are present in the world, so dramatic display is not self-authenticating evidence of the Spirit.

The prophet who presumptuously speaks (yazid, hiphil imperfect from zid, attested 10x with consistent semantic field of proud or insolent self-assertion in Deut 1:43, 17:13, 18:20, Neh 9:10, 9:16, 9:29, Jer 50:29) a word in YHWH's name that was not commanded, or who speaks in the name of other gods, is to die. The criterion fixes attention on the source and authorization of the word, not on its intensity or ecstatic accompaniment.

The empirical test is whether the spoken davar comes to pass and is fulfilled. A word that does not happen marks speech spoken bezadon (in presumption, the cognate noun of zid, attested 11x across Deuteronomy, Samuel, Proverbs, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Obadiah with the same arrogance semantic field). The people are not to fear it. The standard is verification by fulfillment, an external check that bypasses subjective manifestation entirely.

complicating_texts.resolution: The same chapter that commands order also commands me koluete lalein glossais (do not forbid speaking in tongues), so the orderly-worship norm in 14:40 does not suppress the gifts but governs their exercise. The proposition targets treating ecstatic phenomena as the normative standard, not the existence of the gifts, so 14:39 is consistent with the verdict.

Pentecost onlookers mocked the disciples as filled with new wine (G1098 gleukos), which could suggest disorderly appearance. The narrative resolves it lexically: Acts 2:6 reports each one heard them speaking in their own dialektos (G1258, intelligible native language), and Peter then delivers a structured doctrinal address (Acts 2:14-36). The episode therefore models comprehensible, content-bearing speech rather than ecstatic spectacle as the proof of the Spirit. The mockery records an outsider misreading, not the lexical pattern of the event.

Paul caps tongues at two or three (G1417 dyo, G5140 treis), in turn (G3313 meros, G0303 ana), with G1329 diermeneutes (interpreter), and requires silence if none is present. The numerical and procedural limits encoded in these explicit lexemes confirm that even genuine gift-exercise is bounded and orderly, reinforcing rather than complicating the verdict that uncontrolled phenomena are not the norm.

Pneumata propheton prophetais hypotassetai (G5293 hypotasso, present passive). The spirits of prophets are subject to prophets. The lexical claim is direct: prophetic spiritual experience is voluntarily controllable by the prophet, not an overriding force. This forecloses the reading that loss-of-control phenomena are the Spirit's normative signature.

Prophetai de dyo e treis laleitosan, kai hoi alloi diakrinetosan (G1252 diakrino, others judge or evaluate). The very class of utterance most associated with ecstatic immediacy is subjected to community discrimination, parallel to dokimazo in 1 John 4:1 and 1 Thess 5:21. Reinforces the verdict.

variants.note: Cited verses lie outside 3 John CBGM sample scope. The known variant at 1 Cor 14:40 concerns the position of the connective de, which does not touch the euschemonos kai kata taxin clause that carries the verdict, so no variant materially affects the reading. The 1 Cor 14:34-35 interpolation question does not bear on the cited verses.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: A reading that views the miraculous sign-gifts as concluded still affirms the proposition on the same lexical ground, since the order, peace, and testing vocabulary (akatastasia, eirene, euschemonos, taxis, dokimazo, diakrino, hypotasso) describes how the Spirit operates in any era and excludes ecstatic spectacle as the diagnostic of His presence.

A reading that holds the gifts to continue also affirms the proposition in its strongest form: the very chapter that permits tongues (me koluete in 14:39) and prophecy is the same chapter that subordinates them to euschemonos kai kata taxin (14:40), to dokimazo and diakrino testing (1 John 4:1, 1 Cor 14:29), and to hypotasso (14:32, prophets' spirits subject to prophets). Continued operation is therefore consistent with, and in fact requires, orderly and tested exercise. Hyper-charismatic excess as defined here (uncontrolled tongues, false prophecies, manipulative miracles) is what these very texts regulate against.

A position that holds judgment on cessation but applies the New Testament regulation strictly still affirms, because the regulation itself is what the proposition asserts. The lay-summary nuance applies: the texts fix the principle (order and testing) decisively but leave the precise contextual boundary between Spirit-led contribution and disorder to be worked out by the gathered, judging community (14:29).

hermeneutics.notes: All three lenses converge because the verdict turns on the order, peace, and testing word-fields, not on whether sign-gifts persist. The proposition concerns the normative criterion of the Spirit's presence, which the lexical data locates in tested, orderly, fulfillment-verified speech rather than in dramatic phenomena. The remaining lexical underdetermination is scope, not direction: the texts forbid disorder but do not enumerate every contested borderline practice.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: Does the New Testament establish orderly and tested worship as the standard for recognizing the Spirit's presence, or does it present dramatic ecstatic phenomena (falling, sustained laughter, conscience-binding prophetic decrees) as the normative evidence?
stem_audit.notes: The phrase departs from the New Testament pattern of orderly worship presupposes both that an orderly pattern is normative and that ecstatic-centric practice deviates from it, which bundles the conclusion into the stem. The neutralized form poses the question without prejudging which criterion the text endorses. The verdict was still derived on the original stem from the lexical data, which independently supports the order, peace, and testing pattern via akatastasia versus eirene, euschemonos kai kata taxin, hypotasso of prophetic spirits, diakrino by others, dokimazo at 1 John 4:1 and 1 Thess 5:21, and the Deuteronomic zid and zadon plus fulfillment test.

lay_summary: The words in these passages point one direction. In 1 Corinthians 14:33 Paul says God is not a God of disorder (akatastasia) but of peace (eirene). Every other New Testament use of akatastasia is pejorative (riots, instability, factional confusion), so the negative predication is sharp. The chapter closes in 14:40 with a plain command that everything be done decently (euschemonos, used elsewhere only of walking properly toward outsiders) and in order (kata taxin). Just before that, 14:27 caps tongues at two or three, one at a time, with someone to interpret, and tells the speaker to stay silent if no interpreter is present. 14:29 says when prophets speak the others are to judge (diakrino) what is said. 14:32 says directly that the spirits of prophets are subject (hypotasso) to prophets. Loss-of-control is not the Spirit's signature in this text. In 1 John 4:1 the readers are told to test (dokimazo) the spirits to see whether they are from God, because many false prophets have gone out into the world, and 1 Thessalonians 5:21 uses the same verb of prophetic utterance specifically. A powerful display is not by itself proof that the Spirit is at work. The word has to be examined. Deuteronomy 18:20-22 adds the same logic from the older covenant. A prophet who speaks presumptuously (from zid and zadon, words that carry arrogant self-assertion across Deuteronomy, Samuel, Proverbs, Jeremiah) a word that was never commanded is condemned, and the test of a true word is whether it actually comes to pass. The check is fulfillment and authorization, not the intensity of the experience. Reading these texts together, the consistent measure of genuine spiritual speech is that it is orderly, intelligible, subject to testing, and verified by fulfillment. Making dramatic ecstatic phenomena such as falling, sustained laughter, or binding prophetic decrees the standard evidence of the Spirit does not match this pattern. Where readers differ is not the principle but the exact boundary case. The vocabulary fixes that the Spirit operates in order and submits to testing, but it does not enumerate every contested practice, so the gathered community has to judge particulars (14:29 again). Both a view that the sign-gifts have ceased and a view that they continue land in the same place here, because the order, peace, and testing language describes how the Spirit works regardless of which gifts remain in operation.
